text.characters: Warning Signs: Panic Attacks and Panic Disorder

Panic attacks can happen suddenly and feel overwhelming. Many people describe them as intense waves of fear that appear without warning, even when there is no real danger present. While occasional anxiety is a normal part of life, repeated panic attacks may be a sign of panic disorder and should not be ignored.

A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear or discomfort that usually peaks within minutes. During an attack, the body reacts as if it is facing a serious threat, triggering strong physical and emotional symptoms.  Common symptoms may include:
Rapid heartbeat or chest pain
Shortness of breath
Dizziness or feeling faint
Sweating or shaking
Nausea or stomach discomfort
Tingling sensations
Feeling detached from reality
Fear of losing control or dying
Because these symptoms can feel severe, some people mistake panic attacks for heart attacks or other medical emergencies.

Panic disorder occurs when panic attacks happen repeatedly and create ongoing fear about when the next attack might occur. Over time, this fear can affect daily routines, work, social activities, and relationships.  People with panic disorder may begin to:
Avoid crowded places or unfamiliar situations
Stay away from activities that trigger anxiety
Constantly worry about their physical health
Feel anxious even when there is no immediate danger
Without support, panic disorder can gradually reduce a person’s confidence and quality of life.

Some early signs that may indicate panic disorder include:
Frequent unexpected panic attacks
Constant fear of another attack
Avoiding places or situations because of anxiety
Difficulty sleeping due to worry
Increased sensitivity to stress
Trouble concentrating or relaxing
Recognizing these signs early can help people seek support before symptoms become more severe.

Panic attacks and panic disorder can feel frightening, but they are manageable with proper support and care. Learning the warning signs can help individuals and families respond earlier, reduce fear, and take positive steps toward better mental well-being.
